sources.name: Sherwin Wu — OpenAI head of platform engineering (already in corpus)

cards.front: What's the practical difference between batch and streaming inference deployment?
cards.back: Batch: process many requests together on a schedule, optimized for throughput and cost — fine when latency doesn't matter (nightly report generation). Streaming: process each request as it arrives, optimized for low latency — required for interactive chat/agent experiences where a user is waiting.

cards.front: Why does a model-serving layer exist separately from the model itself in production architecture?
cards.back: The serving layer handles request batching, load balancing across replicas, caching, rate limiting, and version routing — concerns that are about running the model reliably at scale, not about the model's intelligence. Conflating the two makes both harder to reason about and scale independently.

cards.front: What is a canary deployment, applied to an AI model or prompt change?
cards.back: Route a small percentage of production traffic to the new model/prompt version while the majority stays on the current one — lets you catch quality regressions on real traffic before a full rollout, with limited blast radius if something's wrong.

cards.front: Why do latency, reliability, and cost trade off against each other in model selection for a production feature?
cards.back: A more capable model is usually slower and more expensive per call; a faster/cheaper model may need more retries or fallback logic to hit the same reliability bar. There's rarely a model that wins on all three — the right choice depends on which constraint is tightest for that specific feature (a real-time chat needs latency; a batch analysis job needs cost efficiency).

cards.front: What does "model versioning" actually protect you against in production?
cards.back: Silent behavior drift — a vendor updating a model behind an API alias, or your own prompt change, subtly altering outputs in ways that don't throw errors but degrade quality. Pinning to a specific version and testing before upgrading is how you catch this before users do.

cards.front: Your AI feature works fine in testing but is unreliable in production under load. What's the first thing to check?
cards.back: Rate limits and timeout handling under concurrency — AI API calls are slow relative to typical web requests, so load that's fine for a normal API can exhaust connection pools or hit provider rate limits fast. Check retry/backoff logic and whether failures degrade gracefully (fallback response) or cascade.

cards.front: Why is a fallback/degraded-mode path a required part of AI production architecture, not a nice-to-have?
cards.back: AI providers have outages and rate limits like any external dependency, but an AI feature failing often means a core user-facing capability just disappears. A defined fallback (cached response, simpler rule-based behavior, clear error state) keeps the product functional instead of broken when the model call fails.

cards.front: What's the role of Docker/containerization specifically for AI model deployment, versus general software?
cards.back: Same core benefit as any software — reproducible environments, dependency isolation — but matters more for AI because of heavy, version-sensitive dependencies (specific CUDA/PyTorch versions, model weight files) that are easy to get subtly wrong outside a pinned container.

cards.front: Why does CI/CD for AI systems need to include evals as a gate, not just standard unit tests?
cards.back: Standard tests check that code doesn't crash and logic is correct; they can't catch "the model's answers got subtly worse" after a prompt or model change. Evals-as-CI-gate (running your eval suite before merge/deploy) is the AI-specific addition that catches quality regression the way unit tests catch functional regression.

cards.front: What's the difference between horizontal scaling for a typical web service and for an AI-serving system?
cards.back: Typical web services scale by adding stateless application replicas behind a load balancer — cheap and fast. AI serving often needs GPU-backed replicas, which are expensive and slower to spin up, so autoscaling has to account for cold-start time and cost much more carefully — over-provisioning is expensive, under-provisioning causes queueing/latency spikes.
